info.name: s5w — File Storage API
info.description:
# s5w — file storage API

Everything an application needs from an s5w instance: put files in, organise them, hand out URLs to them.

## Before the first request

Two values, both from whoever runs the instance:

| variable | |
|---|---|
| `baseUrl` | where it answers — `https://files.example.com`, scheme included, no trailing slash |
| `apiKey` | the key issued for your bucket in the admin panel, `s5w_…` |

Put them in a Postman **environment** rather than in the collection, and the key stays out of anything you export or share.

Then send **Check the key**. A 200 there means both values are right and the rest of the collection will work.

## Authentication

Every `/v1` request carries the key:

```
Authorization: Bearer s5w_9f3c…
```

The collection sends it for you.

**The bucket is not in any URL.** It is decided by the key, so there is no parameter to get wrong and no way to reach a bucket that is not yours — not "checked and rejected", but absent from the protocol.

Keys come in two kinds:

| kind | what it opens |
|---|---|
| **read-only** | `/p/{slug}` delivery and `GET /v1/check` — small enough to ship inside a client app |
| **full** | all of `/v1`: files, folders, uploads, temporary links |

A read-only key on `/v1/files` gets **403**, by design: it is not meant to enumerate the bucket, only to fetch files whose slugs it already knows. **Run this collection with a full key.**

A key is shown once, when it is issued — the service keeps only its hash. A lost key is replaced, never recovered.

## What is in here

| folder | |
|---|---|
| **Folders** | optional grouping that carries public visibility, retention and cache policy for everything inside |
| **Uploading** | one-request upload up to 32 MiB, and a resumable chunked upload with no ceiling |
| **Files** | list, read, rename, move |
| **Temporary links** | signed URLs with an expiry, optionally revocable and download-capped |
| **Delivery** | the three ways a browser actually fetches a file |
| **Errors worth handling** | 401, 404 and 422 on purpose, to show the shape |
| **Cleanup** | removes everything the run created |

## Conventions

- **Lists** answer `{ "meta": …, "data": [ … ] }`, where `meta` is `current`, `size`, `total`, `pages`, `previous`, `next`. Everything else answers a plain object.
- **Errors** answer `{ "code", "message" }`, plus `errors` per field when validation failed.
- **Timestamps** look like `2026-08-17 18:22:04 +00:00`.
- **Files are addressed by a 16-character slug.** Database ids never leave the service.
- **Deleting** answers `204` with an empty body.

## Status codes

| code | when |
|---|---|
| **401** | no `Authorization` header, or the key is unknown |
| **403** | the key is disabled, expired, or read-only where full access is required |
| **404** | no such file, folder or link. On delivery it also covers "not yours" — from outside the two are one answer |
| **409** | the name is taken, or a chunk does not continue the upload |
| **413** | over the bucket quota, or a chunk over 16 MiB |
| **422** | the parameters do not add up: no such folder, bad processing options |

## Running the whole collection

Press **Run** and let it go top to bottom. Each request stores what the next one needs — bucket id, folder name, slug, upload id, link token — and **Cleanup** at the end deletes everything it made, so it can be run again.

Only two requests need you: **Upload a file** and **Upload an image with processing** want a file picked in their Body tab. Everything else, the resumable upload included, runs untouched — and skipping those two does not break the run, because the resumable flow provides the file the later requests use.

request.description:
Answers one question: **is this key still good, and what is behind it?**

The only `/v1` endpoint a read-only key may call. It returns what the holder of the key already knows about itself — its bucket, the level of access, the expiry date, and how much room is left.

Call it at application start and from your health check: it separates *the key died* from *the service is down*.

| code | meaning |
|---|---|
| **200** | the key works |
| **401** | no `Authorization` header, or the key is unknown |
| **403** | the key is disabled or past its expiry date |

Retrying a 403 with the same secret will never help — that key needs to be replaced.

The test attached to this request stores `bucketId`, which the public delivery URL needs.

item.name: Folders
item.description:
Folders are optional: a file can live in the bucket root. What a folder adds is **shared settings for everything inside it** — public visibility, a retention period, a cache policy.

There is one level. Folders do not nest, and a name is unique within a bucket.

The collection creates `{{folderName}}` here and everything after this point uploads into it.

request.description:
`public: true` is what makes the files inside reachable at `/o/{bucketId}/{slug}` without a key. Files uploaded into a public folder are public from the moment they land; flipping the flag later rewrites every file already inside.

`retention` deletes files by age. It is measured from the moment the file is created, and the sweep runs every five minutes, so removal is prompt but not instant.

| value | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | none | day | week | month | quarter | half year | year |

The name may hold letters, digits, spaces, `.`, `_` and `-`, and must start with a letter or a digit. Up to 100 characters.

**409** means the name is taken. The test below treats that as success so the collection can be run more than once.

Full replacement: whatever you leave out goes back to its default, so send all three fields.

Two of them reach the files inside:

- **`public`** rewrites the flag on every file in the folder;
- **`retention`** recomputes the expiry of every file in the folder from its creation date. Moving from `YEAR` to `DAY` can therefore delete files that are already older than a day, on the next sweep.

Renaming to a name another folder holds gives **409**.

request.description:
Decides the `Cache-Control` header the delivery endpoints put on files from this folder. Without it they inherit the bucket policy.

| `visibility` | header | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `1` | `public` | browsers and CDNs may store it |
| `2` | `private` | the browser may, shared caches may not |
| `3` | `no-store` | nobody stores it |

`maxAge` is seconds, `0` … `31536000` (a year).

Send `null` in a field to drop the override and fall back to the bucket policy. Fields you omit stay as they are.

The change lands on the next request for a file — copies already sitting in a CDN keep their old header until it expires.

item.name: Uploading
item.description:
Two ways in, and the choice is about size, not about file type.

| | `POST /v1/files` | `POST /v1/uploads` |
|---|---|---|
| shape | one multipart request | start, then chunks, then finish |
| ceiling | 32 MiB of request body | none |
| survives a broken connection | no, start over | yes, resume from the offset |
| use it for | images, documents, avatars | video, archives, anything over ~30 MiB |

Both accept the same image options and both end with the same file object.

**Deduplication.** Content is stored once per bucket, keyed by its SHA-256. Uploading a file the bucket already holds costs a database row and no disk: the answer comes back with `"deduplicated": true`, its own slug, and its own name. `used_bytes` does not move.

**Names.** A name is unique inside a folder. Upload `report.pdf` twice into the same folder and the second becomes `report (1).pdf` — you get **409** on rename, never on upload.

request.description:
**Pick a file first:** Body → form-data → the `file` row → Select Files.

Multipart, one request. The body carries the file plus whatever of these you need:

| field | |
|---|---|
| `file` | required, the bytes |
| `folder` | folder name; omit it and the file lands in the bucket root. **422** if no such folder |
| `name` | stored name. Defaults to the uploaded file's name |

Answer is **201** with the file object. Take `id` — the 16-character slug — and keep it: it is how the file is addressed everywhere else, including the delivery URLs.

The request body is capped at **32 MiB** in total. Something larger belongs in the resumable flow below, and so does anything sent over a connection you do not trust.

**413** means the bucket quota is full, not that the request is too big.

request.description:
**Pick an image first:** Body → form-data → the `file` row → Select Files.

Same endpoint, four more fields. Processing happens once, at upload time — what is stored is the result, and the original is not kept.

| field | values | |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `ORIGINAL` `WEBP` `JPEG` `PNG` `AVIF` | re-encode. `ORIGINAL` keeps the format |
| `quality` | 1–100 | encoder quality. Default depends on the format: 82, 60 for PNG, 55 for AVIF |
| `maxWidth` | 16–10000 | fit inside this width |
| `maxHeight` | 16–10000 | fit inside this height |

`maxWidth` and `maxHeight` shrink and never enlarge, and the aspect ratio is kept — a 320×200 source under 160×160 comes out 160×100. EXIF rotation is applied, and the rest of the metadata is dropped with the re-encode.

Send none of the four and the bytes are stored exactly as they arrived.

The answer's `processed` block reports what was done. On a non-image it comes back `"applied": false` with a reason instead of an error, so a mixed upload path does not need to branch.

The name follows the format: `photo.png` uploaded as `WEBP` is stored as `photo.webp`.

item.name: Resumable upload
item.description:
Four requests: **start**, **send a chunk** (as many times as it takes), **finish**. The upload survives a dropped connection — ask the server how much it has and continue from there.

| | |
|---|---|
| chunk size | 4 MiB minimum, 16 MiB maximum. The last chunk may be any size |
| suggested | `chunkSize` in the answer to *start*, currently 8 MiB |
| ordering | strictly sequential, no parallel chunks and no gaps |
| lifetime | 24 hours from the last chunk, then the staging file is swept |
| cost | a session in progress does not count against the bucket quota; the finished file does |

Nothing is visible in the bucket until **finish** returns: that is the request that turns staging bytes into a file and gives you a slug.

The size declared at the start is binding — SHA-256 is computed as the chunks arrive and the file is rejected if the total does not match.

**These requests run as they are.** They send a 23-byte chunk of text, which is the one case where a chunk may be under 4 MiB: it is also the last one.

request.description:
Declares what is coming. Everything that can be refused is refused here — before any bytes move: a folder that does not exist, a size the quota cannot hold, a disk without room.

| field | |
|---|---|
| `name` | required, the stored name |
| `size` | required, exact total in bytes |
| `folder` | optional folder name |
| `sha256` | optional, see *Skip the transfer* below |
| `format` `quality` `maxWidth` `maxHeight` | the image options, applied when the upload finishes |

Answer is **201** with `id` — a UUID, the handle for every later request — and `chunkSize`, the size to send.

**413** here means the declared size does not fit in the quota.

request.description:
`offset` is how many bytes the server holds. After a connection dies, ask this and continue from that number — that is the whole resume protocol.

**404** means the session is gone: finished, cancelled, or swept after 24 hours. Start a new one.

header.description: Where this chunk starts. Optional; a mismatch answers 409.

request.description:
The body is the raw bytes of the chunk — not JSON, not multipart. Repeat until `offset` equals `size`.

`Upload-Offset` says where this chunk belongs. It is optional but worth sending: a mismatch comes back as **409** with the offset the server actually has, which turns a duplicated or lost chunk into a retry instead of a corrupted file. Without the header the chunk is simply appended.

| code | |
|---|---|
| **200** | accepted, `offset` in the body is the new position |
| **400** | empty chunk, or under 4 MiB when it is not the last one |
| **409** | `Upload-Offset` does not match the server's position |
| **413** | over 16 MiB, or past the declared total size |

A chunk that arrives twice is not silently ignored — send the offset and let the 409 tell you where you are.

item.name: Skip the transfer with a known hash

request.description:
Hash the file locally, send the hash with the start request, and if that content is already in the bucket the file is created on the spot — no chunks, nothing over the wire.

The answer is the same shape as a normal start, told apart by two fields: `file` is an object instead of `null`, and `chunkSize` is `0`. There is no session to continue and no id to call.

Content the bucket has never seen answers exactly like a normal start, and you upload as usual. So it is always worth sending the hash: it costs one SHA-256 pass over a local file and can save the whole upload.

Lowercase hex, 64 characters. This request reuses the hash of the file from step 4, so it always dedups.

request.description:
Only here so the next request has something to cancel — the session from step 1 is finished and cannot be cancelled any more.

Nothing is sent into this one.

Drops the session and the staging bytes. **204**, empty body.

Optional in practice: an abandoned session is swept 24 hours after its last chunk. Cancelling explicitly just frees the disk now.

**404** — already finished, already cancelled, or already swept.

item.name: Files
item.description:
Everything that is not uploading: finding files, reading one, moving and renaming.

A file is addressed by its **slug** — 16 characters of `A-Za-z0-9-_`, the `id` field of every file object. Database ids never leave the service, so a slug is safe to store, log and put in a URL.

query.description: Exact folder name. Empty means the whole bucket.

request.description:
Paged, one bucket, newest first by default.

| parameter | |
|---|---|
| `page` | from 1 |
| `limit` | 1–100, default 25 |
| `search` | part of a name |
| `folder` | exact folder name. Omit for the whole bucket |
| `sort` | `created` `name` `type` `size` |
| `dir` | `asc` `desc` |

Empty parameters are ignored, so leaving `search` blank is the same as not sending it.

There is no "root only" filter: `folder` narrows to one folder, and no `folder` means everything.

`name` renames, `folder` moves. Both travel together, and both are replaced by what you send — omitting `folder` moves the file to the bucket root.

item.name: Temporary links
item.description:
A signed URL that serves one file, to someone who has no key, until it expires.

The token is signed, so nothing about it can be edited from outside: change one character and it stops verifying. Everything the link is allowed to do is baked in at issue time.

**Two kinds, and the difference matters.**

| | one-off (stateless) | revocable |
|---|---|---|
| how to get it | `ttl` only | `revocable: true`, or any `maxDownloads` |
| stored | nothing | a row |
| `id` in the answer | `null` | a number |
| can be revoked | no, it lives out its `ttl` | yes, one by one or all at once |
| counts downloads | no | yes, and can be capped |

A one-off link costs nothing to issue — issue millions. A revocable one is a row you can kill later.

`ttl` is seconds, up to 30 days. `maxDownloads` up to 1000; a `304 Not Modified` does not count as a download.

request.description:
| field | |
|---|---|
| `ttl` | required, seconds until it expires. 1 … 2592000 (30 days) |
| `disposition` | `0` opens in the browser, `1` forces a download |
| `revocable` | `true` stores the link so it can be revoked |
| `maxDownloads` | 1–1000, implies a stored link |
| `note` | up to 255 characters, for your own bookkeeping. Never shown to whoever opens the link |

Answer is **201** with `url` — hand that out as it is; the host in it follows `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` on the instance.

Revoking is what this collection needs, so it asks for a stored link.

No `revocable`, no `maxDownloads` — nothing is written down. The token carries the file, the expiry and the disposition, and the signature makes it unforgeable.

`id` comes back `null`: there is no row, so there is nothing to revoke and no download counter. It dies when `ttl` runs out.

This is the one to use for links you hand out in bulk — a page of thumbnails, an email with attachments, a signed URL per request.

If you do need to kill these, **Revoke every link in the bucket** invalidates one-off links too: it moves the bucket's signing epoch, and every token issued before that stops verifying.

item.name: Delivery
item.description:
Three ways to hand a file to a browser. All of them stream, support `Range`, send an `ETag` and answer `304` to a conditional request, and none of them touch the `/v1` API.

| | who may fetch it | when to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `/o/{bucketId}/{slug}` | anyone | assets a CDN should cache: images on a public page, avatars, downloads |
| `/p/{slug}` | a key, either kind | a client app that already carries a read-only key |
| `/t/{token}` | whoever holds the link | a file for one recipient, for a while |

`/o` only serves files that are actually public — a private file answers **404** there, the same 404 a missing file gets. From outside, "not yours" and "not here" are one answer.

Add `?download=1` to `/o` or `/p` to send `Content-Disposition: attachment` instead of showing the file in the browser.

**Caching.** `Cache-Control` comes from the folder policy, then the bucket policy. Every hit is counted as egress for the bucket.

request.description:
No key, no header — this URL is the whole credential, which is why only public files are served here.

`bucketId` is the UUID from **Check the key**; the file object hands you the same URL ready-made in `publicUrl`.

**404** — the file is private, was deleted, or never existed.

request.description:
`Range: bytes=0-9` asks for the first ten bytes. The answer is **206** with `Content-Range: bytes 0-9/23`.

This is what makes a `<video>` seek and a download resume: the player asks for the piece it needs instead of the whole file.

One range per request. A range past the end of the file answers **416**.

Same bytes, same caching. The parameter only changes what the browser does with them.

Serves any file in the bucket the key belongs to, public or not. A **read-only key is enough** — this is the endpoint a mobile or single-page app is meant to use with a key that is allowed to do nothing else.

No bucket in the URL: it comes from the key, as everywhere in this API.

`?download=1` works here too.

For a link with `maxDownloads`, this is the request that spends one. A `304` does not count — nothing was transferred.

**404** covers everything that can be wrong with a link: expired, revoked, out of downloads, signed before the bucket's links were purged, or simply mistyped. The reason is deliberately not disclosed.

item.name: Errors worth handling
item.description:
Three requests that fail on purpose, so the shape of a failure is visible before your code meets one.

Errors are always `{ "code", "message" }`, with `errors` added per field when validation is what failed. `code` repeats the HTTP status — read the status, and use `message` for your logs, not for your control flow.

request.description:
Authentication is switched off for this request only, so it goes out without the `Authorization` header.

**401** is *the service does not know you*. Sending the same request with a valid key fixes it.

**403** is a different thing: the key is known and refused — disabled, past its expiry, or read-only on an endpoint that needs full access. Retrying that one never helps.

A slug that is well-formed and belongs to no file here.

A slug from another bucket answers exactly the same way. Nothing in the API tells you whether a file exists somewhere else.

An empty folder name. Validation answers **422** with `errors`: a field name against the list of rules it broke.

That is the object to map onto your form fields. The top-level `message` stays generic on purpose.

item.name: Cleanup
item.description:
Removes what the run above created, so the collection can be run again and leaves nothing behind.

Deletion is immediate for the database row. The bytes go when nothing points at them any more: two files sharing content keep it alive until both are gone, and a nightly sweep collects what is left unreferenced.

request.description:
Kills one stored link. **204**, and `/t/{token}` for it answers 404 from the next request on.

Only stored links have an id — a one-off link cannot be revoked this way. **404** means no link with that id in this bucket.

item.name: Revoke every link in the bucket

request.description:
The big red button: **every** temporary link of this bucket stops working, stored and one-off alike.

It works by moving the bucket's signing epoch, which is part of what each token is signed with — so tokens that were never written down anywhere die too. Files, folders and keys are untouched.

The answer is the new `epoch`.

**204**, empty body. The slug is gone from every delivery endpoint at once.

Links pointing at the file are not cleaned up here; they answer 404 because the file is missing.

Deleting a file that never existed is **404**, so a delete is not idempotent — treat 404 on retry as success.

**Deletes the files inside it too.** There is no "move them to the root" mode and no confirmation step — this is the one destructive request in the collection.

**204** on success, **404** if the folder is already gone.
